Problem: Algorithms - 18
P3
Suppose G = (V, E) is a connected graph with weighted edges. Establish that for any
P4
cycle in G, the maximum-weight edge of that cycle is not included in the minimum
P5
spanning tree of G.
P6
Solution:
Proof. Let T be a minimum spanning tree of the weighted graph G. Consider any cycle C
in G. Choose an edge emax ∈C whose weight is maximum among the edges of C (if multiple
edges in C share the maximum weight, choose one arbitrarily). We claim that emax cannot
belong to T.
Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that emax ∈T. Since T is a spanning tree, it
contains no cycles; therefore T **does not** contain all the edges of C. In particular, there
is at least one edge of C that is *not* in T. Let f be any edge of C with f /∈T.
Now, T is a tree on all vertices of G, so removing the edge emax from T will disconnect
the graph into exactly two components (trees). Let U and W denote the vertex sets of these
two components when emax is deleted. (Intuitively, U and W are the two “sides” of the
**cut** created by removing emax.) By construction, emax had one endpoint in U and the
other endpoint in W, and after removing emax no edge of T connects a vertex in U to a
vertex in W.
Consider the cycle C in the original graph G. The edge emax was part of cycle C, so
if we remove emax from C, the remaining edges of C form a path in G connecting the two
endpoints of emax. That is, there is a path P in G from some vertex u ∈U to some vertex
v ∈W consisting of all the edges of C except emax. Since u ∈U and v ∈W, this path P
must cross from U to W at least once. Therefore, along P, there exists some edge f that
connects a vertex in U to a vertex in W. (In fact, the first time the path P leaves U and
enters W, it uses such an edge f.) By the definition of U and W, no such U–W edge lies in
T (otherwise U and W would not have been separate components when emax was removed).
Hence this edge f we found on P is one of the edges missing from T, and indeed we have
f ∈C with f /∈T, as chosen above.
Now, let us add the edge f to the forest T −{emax}.
Adding f reconnects the two
components U and W, because f directly joins a vertex of U to a vertex of W. Moreover,
adding f does not create any cycle in T −{emax}: since T −{emax} had no path between
U and W, the new edge f provides the only route between those two sets.
Therefore,
�T −{emax}
∪{f} is again a spanning tree of G. (In fact, T ′ is a spanning tree that
differs from T by removing emax and replacing it with f.)
We now compare the total weights. Let w(e) denote the weight of an edge e. By our
choice of emax, we have w(f) ≤w(emax). Therefore, the total weight of T ′ is
w(T ′) = w(T) −w(emax) + w(f) ≤w(T) .
In fact, if emax was strictly heavier than the other edges in C (so w(f) < w(emax)), then
w(T ′) < w(T). But T was assumed to be a minimum spanning tree of G, so it cannot
have a higher weight than some other spanning tree. This is a contradiction. Even in the
case w(f) = w(emax), we see that w(T ′) = w(T), which means T ′ is also a minimum-weight
spanning tree of G. In particular, we have shown that there is a minimum spanning tree T ′
which does **not** contain emax.
In all cases, we conclude that our assumption was wrong: the edge emax (the heaviest
edge of cycle C) cannot be part of any minimum spanning tree. Since C was an arbitrary
cycle in G, this proves that for every cycle in G, the maximum-weight edge of that cycle
is absent from the minimum spanning tree. (This fundamental fact is often known as the
**cycle property** of MSTs.)
